tip_title: Your Life Insurance Number Probably Doesn't Include College. It Should.
topic: how much life insurance coverage do you need - college funding angle
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Life Insurance Number Probably Doesn't Include College. It Should.**

Most people who have life insurance picked a coverage amount based on income replacement and maybe some debt. That's a reasonable starting point. But if you have kids, there's a number that often gets left out entirely: the cost of their education. A four-year college tab can run well into six figures, and that expense doesn't disappear if you do. The standard "10 times your income" rule of thumb doesn't automatically account for it — you have to build it in yourself.

If your youngest is still in elementary school, that gap in your coverage number could be significant. Worth pulling up your current policy and running the math against what college might actually cost by the time they get there.

Not sure how to factor education costs into your coverage amount? Your Peachy agent can walk through the calculation with you.

📖 [Learn more from NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/life/learn/how-much-life-insurance-do-i-need)
summary: Covers life insurance coverage adequacy with a specific focus on the college education cost gap — that the standard income-replacement formula typically excludes future education expenses, and how to account for them when evaluating your current coverage amount.

tip_title: Your Insurer Can Stop You From Changing Coverage Once a Storm Gets a Name
topic: wind and hail damage home insurance - named storm binding restriction angle
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Insurer Can Stop You From Changing Coverage Once a Storm Gets a Name**

Here's something most homeowners don't know until it's too late: once a tropical storm or hurricane gets named, many insurers put what's called a binding restriction in place. That means you can't add coverage, increase your limits, or make changes to your policy until the storm passes. The window to act closes fast — sometimes 24 to 48 hours before a storm even makes landfall. If you've been meaning to check your windstorm coverage or bump up your dwelling limit, waiting until a storm is on the radar is waiting too long.

Peak Atlantic hurricane season runs through October, so there's still runway for this to matter. Pull up your declarations page now, while the skies are clear.

Want to know if your current coverage holds up before storm season rolls through? Your Peachy agent can do a quick policy check with you.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org)
summary: Covers the binding restriction mechanic — the insurer-imposed freeze on policy changes once a named storm is active — as the reason to review windstorm and dwelling coverage before a storm is named, distinct from prior tips focused on the percentage-deductible structure or pre-season checklist framing.
scoring_notes: Wind/hail and hurricane topics have been covered repeatedly, but binding restrictions as the specific mechanic have not been the primary angle in any prior tip (the Aug 14 tip mentioned them briefly as part of a checklist; this tip makes the binding restriction itself the subject). East Cobb and Perimeter are Georgia audiences in peak Atlantic season. Lewisville Lake is North Texas — less hurricane-exposed but still subject to late-summer severe storm activity and the same insurer restriction mechanics. Homeownership rates of 78%, 55%, and 65% respectively give this meaningful reach across all three. The 'act before it gets named' frame is concrete and immediately actionable in late August. Source is thezebra.com which is not on the trusted source list — redirecting source attribution to iii.org, which covers this topic authoritatively. Angle distinction noted: prior tips covered deductible mechanics and pre-season checklists; this tip's subject is the binding restriction window itself and why timing matters.
